doc.title: Derek Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

chapter: Studio work and the Basie connection
title: Playing with the Basie band for Sammy Cahn; Basie alumni in the studios
summary: He accompanied Sammy Cahn with the Basie band, and discusses Basie sidemen in studios and the decline of studio work.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Have you had occasion to play with the Basie band?

Look, the only time I played with the Basie band, and that’s cheating really, I was accompanying Sammy Cahn who was a songwriter of some repute, and Sam would do an act and get a lot of money for playing this act in various parts of the country. So one day Sam called and he’d say, “oh we’ve got this gig in Chicago.” So I says, “fine.” He says, “it’s with the Basie band.” I said, “what?” He hung up the phone. So we had some arrangements, and I just put them out, and I had to get Count off the piano, raise the piano seat because he had it very low, and we went over it. It was the Basie band, and we played all this stuff for Sam. He wasn’t a very good singer but he wrote all these songs and so people had to take him seriously. So that was the time with the Basie band. But of course all the side men have been my friends for years, because they like Frank Foster and Frank Wess — we were all in the studios together playing all these dog food commercials for years.
Most of those guys that did that, were they, that was after they had had the Basie experience, the big band road thing.
And they decided they wanted to stay in one place for a little while?

Yes. Exactly. And that’s what they did. And at that time you have to realize there was so much work for musicians, and especially if you came out of a big band background. Because most of the music was kind of jazz influenced. And there was always big budgets for commercials and they wanted the band to sound right. And so all these guys were coming off the bands and moving straight into this highly paid studio work. And,

but then of course nothing stays the same forever, and the studio work disappears now, because, well many different reasons. (a) we all got older; (b) technology put us out of work because they can do things with synthesizers where they don’t need so many live musicians anymore. And so then I read that Frank Foster is back on the road now leading the band.
Yeah. We had a nice interview with him a couple of months ago with Bill Hughes. Tell us about working with Benny Goodman.
